scenario: You raised BTN, BB calls. Flop A♦7♣2♥ (dry, disconnected). You have Q♠J♠ (nothing).
question: Should you c-bet this dry ace-high board even with nothing?
explanation: C-bet. The A-7-2 rainbow board hits YOUR range (you have the aces, BB would 3-bet AA/AK) and misses the BB's capped calling range. High fold equity + range advantage = textbook c-bet bluff, even holding QJ. Board texture + range advantage drive this, not your cards. Yes — dry ace-high board favors your raising range; BB's capped range whiffs, high fold equity.

scenario: You raised, and got THREE callers. Flop 9♥8♥7♣ (very wet, multiway). You have A♠A♦ (overpair).
question: How does multiway + wet board change your overpair c-bet?
explanation: Number of opponents + vulnerability are key factors. AA is strong, but 9-8-7 two-tone with THREE opponents is dangerous — straights, two pair, sets, flush draws all live in those ranges. Hardin: bet for value+protection to deny equity, but your overpair's relative strength is much lower multiway. Don't stack off light. This is exactly the 'overvaluing one pair' trap on a wet multiway board. Bet for value AND protection — but be ready to fold to heavy action; multiway wet boards crush overpairs often.

scenario: You raised, one caller. Flop K♠K♦4♣ (paired, dry). You have A♥Q♥ (ace-high).
question: Paired dry board, you have ace-high. C-bet or check?
explanation: C-bet bluff. Paired dry boards (K-K-4) are premium c-bet bluffing spots: the caller rarely holds the trips (few Kx in a flat-call range), your range credibly contains kings and overpairs, and most of their range (small pairs, broadway misses) folds. Board texture + range advantage = bet, despite ace-high. C-bet — paired dry boards favor the aggressor's range and are great bluff spots; caller rarely has a king, folds most of their range.

scenario: You raised BTN, the BB (a calling station, fold-to-cbet 25%) calls. Flop 6♠5♠4♦ (wet, low). You have A♣K♦ (two overcards, no pair, no draw).
question: Against a station on a wet low board with AK-high, c-bet?
explanation: When NOT to c-bet: low fold equity + board favors their range + you have no made hand/draw. A 6-5-4 board hits a station's wide range hard (any two pair, straight, draw), and a 25% fold-to-cbet means they won't fold. Firing AK-high here has no value (worse doesn't call) and no fold equity (they don't fold). Check. Opponent tendency + board texture override 'AK is pretty.' No — wet board smashes a station's wide calling range, and they don't fold (25% fold-to-cbet); no fold equity, no made hand.

scenario: YOUR HAND. You 3-bet with QJs and reach a flop A-J-7 with middle pair (the J). You CHECK the flop as the aggressor, out of position (pot control). Turn is a blank.
question: You checked flop with middle pair on an ace-high board. Was that check correct, and what now?
explanation: Based on your real QJs hand. Checking middle pair OOP on an ace-high board is a defensible pot-control play — one pair, mediocre kicker, out of position, against a range that still holds better jacks, sets, and the ace itself. That's real showdown value, but not a hand that gains much from barrelling: a raise makes you fold anyway, so betting mostly just risks chips to fold out worse jacks and busted overcards. One caveat on the reasoning, not the conclusion: this isn't really about 'the ace favoring the caller' — in 3-bet pots the ace often favors YOUR range more, since most weak aces get folded to a 3-bet before the flop ever happens. The real case for checking is simpler — OOP, medium strength, nothing extra to protect, so take a cheap look and decide later. Calling this a 'delayed c-bet' is also a bit of a stretch: that term normally describes checking IN POSITION and betting later once you've seen a free card; OOP, you're not delaying anything, you're just checking. The actual leak in the real hand came later — calling big bets with one pair — not from this initial check.

scenario: You raise CO, BTN (a thinking TAG) calls — you are OUT of position. Flop A♠T♦6♣. You have K♣Q♦ (no pair, gutshot to the broadway).
question: OOP vs a TAG on A-T-6 with KQ gutshot. C-bet?
options: Check — no pair, no business betting
Bet big to protect your equity
Small c-bet, then keep barreling if called
explanation: Position is a c-bet factor. The A-T-6 board favors your range (you have the aces), so a small c-bet as a range bet is fine -- and KQ has a gutshot + backdoors, so it's not pure air either. But you're OOP with no made hand: plan to give up if raised, or if called and you don't improve. Checking gives up a profitable range bet for no reason; a big bet risks more than the hand justifies; barreling multiple streets without equity is the classic OOP-overcommitment leak. C-bet small once, then proceed honestly based on what happens next.

scenario: You raise, get TWO callers. Flop J♥T♥9♠ (extremely wet, multiway). You have A♠A♦ (overpair, no heart).
question: Overpair on a super-wet multiway board (J-T-9 two-tone). C-bet?
options: Bet big for value — it's aces
explanation: Multiway + extreme wetness downgrades even aces. J-T-9 two-tone connects with two callers' ranges enormously: KQ/Q8/87 straights, sets, two pair, combo draws. Your AA holds ONE pair with no heart — its relative strength multiway is poor. This is the overvaluing-one-pair trap in its purest form. Bet small for protection at most, and be fully prepared to fold to significant action. Do not stack off a single pair here. Check or bet small with give-up plan — this board crushes two callers' ranges (straights, two pair, sets, flush+straight draws); AA is now a vulnerable one-pair hand multiway.

scenario: You raise UTG, BB calls. Flop K♦ 7♠ 2♣ (dry, disconnected, rainbow). You have 9♠ 8♠ (nothing, backdoor spade draw).
question: Dry king-high board, your UTG range vs BB's flatting range — c-bet with nothing?
explanation: C-bet small. UTG's opening range is loaded with big cards and pairs that connect with K-7-2, while BB's flatting range (suited connectors, small pairs, weak kings) mostly misses or holds something too weak to continue. Range advantage plus a backdoor spade draw is more than enough to fire a small, high-frequency bet — you don't need a made hand when the board itself does the work. Bet small — UTG's range dominates this dry king-high board and BB folds a lot; the backdoor draw is a bonus, not the reason to bet.

scenario: You raise CO, a tight-passive BB (folds to c-bet 78% of the time, rarely continues without a real hand) calls. Flop Q♣ 8♦ 3♥ (dry, rainbow). You have 6♣ 5♣ (nothing, backdoor flush + backdoor straight).
question: You have 6-5 with backdoors only — no pair, no live draw. Against a nit folding to c-bets 78% of the time, what's the right play?
explanation: Opponent tendency can outweigh hand strength as a factor. A 78% fold-to-cbet rate on a dry Q-8-3 board means most of this player's range folds regardless of what you hold — close to a bet-any-two-cards spot. Your backdoor flush and gutshot are a nice bonus if called, but they're not the reason to bet; the read is. Bet — an extremely high fold-to-cbet stat on a dry board makes your two cards almost irrelevant; you're betting the opponent, not your hand.

scenario: You raise BTN, BB calls. Effective stacks are 22bb. Flop J♥ 8♣ 4♠ (dry-ish, rainbow). You have A♠ J♠ (top pair, top kicker).
question: Short effective stacks (22bb), you flop top pair top kicker — c-bet, or check to control the pot?
explanation: Stack depth is a real c-bet factor, and it cuts the opposite way from what many players assume. At 22bb, there isn't enough room left behind for a scary multi-street escalation to actually threaten you — you're often pot-committed with TPTK by the turn regardless. Pot control matters far more when stacks are deep and the downside of a big pot is large; short, it barely matters. Bet — with stacks this short, TPTK wants to build the pot and get to showdown or an all-in, not shrink it.

scenario: You raise CO, BTN calls. Flop 9♠ 6♠ 2♥ (two-tone spades, low). You have A♠ 4♥ (ace-high, nothing else, but the ace of spades).
question: You hold the ace of spades — no pair, no real draw of your own — on a two-spade flop. Does that blocker change anything about c-betting?
options: No — need a pair or better
explanation: Blockers are a real, if smaller, factor. Holding the A♠ doesn't give you a draw, but it removes the single most threatening combo (the nut flush draw) from BTN's continuing range, and makes it slightly less likely they have two spades at all. Combined with a reasonably dry underlying structure (9-6-2, no straight threats), that's enough to lean toward a bluff here rather than an automatic check. Bet — the ace of spades blocks BTN's best two-tone hands, tipping a close spot toward a bluff.

scenario: You raise BTN, BB calls. Flop K♠ 9♦ 4♣ (dry). You have Q♥ J♥ (ace-high—no, king-high—no: queen-high with a gutshot to the broadway and a backdoor heart draw).
question: Borderline hand — no pair, but a gutshot (any T) plus a backdoor flush draw. Does the extra equity change a close c-bet decision?
options: No — too thin to matter here
No — need a pair at minimum
Yes — it's strong enough to bet for value
explanation: Range advantage alone (you have kings, BB's range is capped) already makes this a lean-bet spot; the gutshot plus backdoor flush just adds enough extra equity to make betting the clear default instead of a coinflip decision. It's not a value bet — QJ isn't ahead of much — but as a semi-bluff with real backup equity, it's a profitable c-bet where a pure air hand might be more marginal. Bet — range advantage plus a real (if thin) equity backup is enough to make this a clean semi-bluff, not a value bet.

scenario: You 3-bet from the BB, BTN calls. Flop A♣ T♠ 6♥ (ace-high, dry). You have K♥ Q♥ (nothing, backdoor flush + gutshot).
question: 3-bet pot, ace-high flop, you whiffed completely. Does being the 3-bettor change how often you should c-bet here versus a normal single-raised pot?
options: Bet more — you keep more aces
Bet less — caller's range is stronger here
No — always check air out of position
explanation: In 3-bet pots, ace-high boards usually favor the 3-bettor, not the caller — most players fold their weaker aces (A9, A8, and worse) to a 3-bet before the flop ever happens, while a 3-betting range plausibly still holds real Ax value (AK, AQ, sometimes AJ) alongside bluffs like this KQ. That's the opposite of the instinct that 'the ace hits the caller.' Bet small and often — 3-bet pots on ace-high boards are a classic spot to c-bet at high frequency, precisely because your own range is the one more likely to hold the ace.

scenario: Two players limp, you raise from the CO (isolating). Only the first limper (a wide, passive limp-caller) calls. Flop J♠ 6♣ 3♦ (dry, disconnected). You have 8♣ 7♣ (nothing, backdoor flush + backdoor straight).
question: You isolated a limper whose range is capped (almost never limp-raises with a big hand). What's your c-bet frequency on this flop?
options: Bet less often — could still be strong
Bet more than usual — the range is capped
Check — a limper could have anything
explanation: Preflop action shapes ranges just as much as the board does. A player who limps and then just calls a raise (rather than 3-betting) is very unlikely to be sitting on AA/KK/AK — those hands usually raise. Their range is wide but weak on a J-6-3 board, which makes this an easy, high-frequency c-bet even with zero pair equity. Bet — the limp-call line caps this opponent's range hard, and a dry disconnected flop mostly misses what's left of it.

scenario: You raise BTN, BB calls. Flop K♦ 8♣ 2♠ (dry, rainbow, favors your range heavily). You have 4♠ 4♥ (bottom pair-ish pocket pair, no draw).
question: This board strongly favors your range as a pure range bet. What sizing fits that plan best?
explanation: Sizing is part of the c-bet decision, not an afterthought. On boards this dry and this favorable to your range, the correct plan is usually to bet SMALL across almost your entire range — a 25–35% bet still gets folds from most of what BB is holding, and betting small lets you do this with a much wider range (including thin pairs like 44) without risking much when called. A big bet here would just be overpaying for fold equity you already had cheaply. Bet small and often — the range advantage does the work; a big sizing would only add unnecessary risk for very little extra fold equity.

scenario: You raise BTN, BB calls. Flop 9♠ 9♦ 4♣ (paired, dry). You have A♥ A♠ (overpair, now effectively trips-adjacent since you block none of the 9s but hold a huge overpair).
question: A paired 9-9-4 board, one caller, you hold aces. Bet big or small?
options: Bet big — near the effective nuts here
Check — paired boards are too dangerous
Bet small — stay cautious just in case
Bet, then auto-fold to any raise
explanation: Not every paired board is scary — a low, dry pair like 9-9-4 rarely improves a single caller's range into something that beats an overpair; very few flatting hands contain a 9, and there's no realistic straight or flush draw here at all. Against one opponent, AA is close to the effective nuts on this specific texture. Bet big — low dry paired boards are one of the best spots to get real value and protection with an overpair; don't shrink the bet out of a generic fear of 'paired boards.'

scenario: You raise CO, only the BB calls (heads-up pot). Flop Q♣ 7♠ 3♥ (dry, rainbow). You have K♠ T♠ (king-high, backdoor spade draw).
question: Heads-up, dry board, king-high with nothing but backdoors — does facing just one opponent make this an easier bluff than it would be multiway?
options: No — opponent count is irrelevant here
No — you should never bluff with air
Yes — but only if you also have a pair
explanation: Fold equity shrinks fast with each extra opponent — needing everyone to fold gets harder the more people are in the hand. Heads-up, you only need one range to fold often enough, and a capped, dry-board-missing BB range does exactly that. The same king-high hand that's a clear bet heads-up becomes far more marginal against two or three callers. Bet — heads-up is the easiest number of opponents to bluff profitably; this same hand gets much worse multiway.

scenario: A very tight UTG player min-raises, BB (also tight) just calls. You're watching this hand as a study example. Flop K♠ J♥ 6♣ (looks scary — two broadway cards). BB's likely holding, given they didn't 3-bet a tight UTG open, is capped well below AA/KK/AK.
question: The flop LOOKS dangerous (two broadway cards), but what does BB's preflop action (just calling a tight UTG open) tell you about c-betting this board as UTG?
options: Board danger is all that matters here
BB definitely has AK, so check
Bet freely — their range is capped
Preflop action never affects postflop reads
explanation: A board can look scary in the abstract while still being a good c-bet, once you account for what the caller's range actually contains. A tight player who flats a tight UTG open (instead of 3-betting) has almost certainly already discarded AA, KK, and usually AK/AQ — exactly the hands that would make K-J-6 dangerous for the raiser. Bet — read the range the preflop action actually leaves behind, not just the raw texture; a capped range makes even a broadway-heavy flop a good c-bet.

scenario: You raise BTN, BB calls. Flop J♠ T♠ 4♥ (two-tone, one gap). You have J♥ 9♥ (top pair, plus a flush draw of your own on a different suit — no, correction: you have the flush draw live on hearts, top pair of jacks).
question: Top pair with a flush draw of your own, on a two-tone board where BB could easily have a spade draw too. Bet small to keep the pot manageable, or bet big to charge draws?
options: Bet small — no need to inflate
Bet big only vs a station
explanation: When you actually have a made hand with real equity to protect — not just a range-advantage bluff — the correct response to a draw-heavy board is to size UP, not down. Betting big charges BB's flush draw and any weaker jack close to the price they need, and it builds a pot you're happy to have with a hand this strong on this texture. Bet big — you have a genuine hand and real protection needs here; this is a value-and-protection spot, not a cheap range bet.

scenario: You raise SB, BB calls (a wide, unselective calling range from BB in this matchup). Flop A♠ 8♣ 3♠ (dry, rainbow). You have K♣ K♥ (overpair, second-nut pair).
question: You have KK, an overpair below the ace, on a dry ace-high board. What's your play?
options: Check — an ace out is too scary
explanation: An ace on board doesn't automatically neuter a big pocket pair — it only matters if the opponent's range contains enough actual aces to worry about. Against a wide, unselective BB calling range, most of what continues is worse pairs, ace-high, and draws, all of which KK beats. Bet for value and protection — don't let 'there's an ace out there' override the fact that most hands that can call still lose to kings; just stay alert if a wide range suddenly gets aggressive.

scenario: You raise CO, BB calls (BB folds to c-bet 70%+, and you hold blockers: A♠ K♠ on a board with two spades). Flop Q♠ 8♠ 4♥ (two-tone, dry underneath). You have nothing but ace-king with the nut flush blocker.
question: Fold equity is high, range favors you, AND you block the nut flush — three factors stacking in the same direction. How confidently should you c-bet?
options: Not at all — no pair overrides it
Only with a backdoor draw too
explanation: None of these factors alone would be a slam dunk, but they compound: a high fold-to-cbet read means most hands fold regardless of texture; range advantage means your continuing range is also stronger than BB's; and holding the nut flush blocker specifically removes their best bluff-catcher/redraw. When factors stack instead of conflict, that's exactly when to bet with the most confidence and frequency, not less. Bet with full confidence — stacked, agreeing factors are the strongest version of a c-bet spot; this is close to a mandatory bluff.

scenario: You raise UTG (narrow range), BB defends (wide range, standard defense). Flop 8♥ 7♠ 6♣ (low, connected, rainbow). You have Q♣ Q♥ (overpair).
question: A narrow UTG range meeting a wide BB defending range on a low connected board — does 'you raised, so you have range advantage' still apply here?
options: Yes — raiser always has the edge
Yes — only due to the overpair
No — this board favors BB's range
explanation: Range advantage isn't automatic just because you raised — it depends on which range fits the board. UTG's range is high-card-heavy and skips right past 8-7-6; BB's wide defending range is full of exactly the suited connectors, one-gappers, and small pairs that smash this texture into two pair, straights, and sets. QQ is still a real hand, but this is a bet-small-or-check spot, not a confident value bet. Check or bet small with a give-up plan — this board is one of the rare textures where the caller's range is actually stronger than the raiser's.

scenario: You raise, get called by THREE players. Flop K♠ 6♥ 2♣ (fairly dry, rainbow). You have Q♥ J♥ (nothing, backdoor flush + gutshot).
question: Three callers, a fairly dry board, you have nothing. Does the dry texture make this a good bluff anyway?
options: Yes — dry boards are always good
No — the hand type is too weak
explanation: Board texture and number of opponents are separate factors, and a bad number of opponents can override an otherwise-good texture. Even on a dry flop, getting three different ranges to all fold at once is much harder than getting one to fold — someone is statistically likely to have connected with a king, a pocket pair, or overs worth continuing with. Check — three-way pots need a real hand or a real draw to bet profitably; dry texture alone doesn't rescue a pure bluff against this many opponents.

scenario: You raise BTN, BB calls. Flop Q♠ 9♠ 4♠ (monotone spades). You have A♥ Q♥ (top pair, top kicker, no spade at all).
question: Monotone flop, you have top pair top kicker but zero spades yourself. C-bet as normal?
options: No — no blockers, play it safe
Yes — bet big to charge it
explanation: Monotone boards are the one texture where 'range advantage' arguments break down fastest — with three of one suit already out, a made flush is live in a meaningful slice of any calling range, and you hold zero blockers to it. TPTK is still a fine hand to get to showdown with, but firing big bets you can't comfortably continue against is the leak. Check or bet small — a good hand with no blockers on a monotone board should play for pot control, not maximum value, until you know more.

scenario: You raise, a loose-passive calling station calls. Flop J♠ T♥ 4♣ (two-tone, connected). You have 8♥ 6♥ (gutshot only — needs exactly a 9 — no overcards, no flush draw of your own suit that matters here).
question: A weak gutshot, no overcards, against a station who never folds. C-bet as a semi-bluff?
options: Yes — any draw is worth a bet
No — no fold equity, weak draw
Yes — bet big to fold out flushes
explanation: Semi-bluffing needs at least one of two things to work: fold equity, or good enough equity/implied odds to justify the money on its own. A calling station supplies neither the fold equity (they don't fold) nor is a single lone gutshot (4 outs, no overcards) strong enough equity to bet purely for value either. Check — against a no-fold opponent, a weak draw like this should take a free or cheap card, not build the pot with a bet that accomplishes nothing.

scenario: Effective stacks are 220bb (very deep). You raise, one caller. Flop K♥ T♠ 9♠ (drawy, two-tone). You have A♣ K♣ (top pair, weak-ish kicker relative to the deep stacks, no spade).
question: Very deep stacks, top pair on a drawy two-tone board with a mediocre kicker for the depth. Bet as usual?
options: Yes — bet bigger since it's deep
No — deep stacks need pot control
explanation: Stack depth cuts both ways depending on the hand — short stacks favor building the pot with top pair (session cbd_10), but very deep stacks do the opposite: the more money that can go in behind, the more dangerous it is to inflate a pot with a vulnerable one-pair hand on a coordinated board, since a determined opponent has the room to make you pay for being wrong. Check for pot control — this is exactly the kind of spot where 'stack off with one pair, deep, on a drawy board' turns into the costliest recurring leak in a player's game.

scenario: You 3-bet from the BB, BTN calls. Flop 8♠ 7♥ 6♠ (low, connected, two-tone). You have A♥ K♣ (ace-king, no pair, no draw).
question: 3-bet pot again — but this time the flop is low and very connected instead of ace-high. Does the general '3-bet pots favor the aggressor' rule still hold?
options: No — this board favors BTN's range
explanation: The '3-bet pots favor the aggressor' heuristic comes from range construction, not from being the 3-bettor by title — it holds on ace-high and king-high boards because those cards concentrate in the 3-bettor's range. A low, connected board flips that: BTN's flatting range (suited connectors, pocket pairs) hits 8-7-6 far harder than a range full of big cards and premium pairs does. Check/give up — don't blanket-apply the ace-high lesson to every 3-bet-pot board; the specific texture still decides whose range it favors.

scenario: You raise, one caller (a very straightforward, 'face-up' player who calls with any pair or draw and basically never bluffs or folds a draw once in). Flop J♠ T♥ 8♣ (very wet, connected). You have 4♠ 3♣ (nothing, no blockers to anything relevant).
question: Wet, connected board, a caller who never folds a pair or a draw, and your hand blocks nothing useful. C-bet?
options: No — no fold equity, no blockers
Yes — bet big to fold out draws
explanation: A wet board is only a good bluffing texture when it also produces folds — against a player who calls any pair or draw and won't fold once committed, the same board that scares off a normal range does nothing here. Your hand also blocks none of their likely holdings (no jack, ten, or eight, no relevant suit), so there's no added leverage either. Check — fold equity is the actual engine behind a bluff; without it, board texture and blockers can't save the bet.

scenario: You raise, BB (a player you've tagged as tight preflop, but who you've also seen call down very wide and never fold once they see a flop) calls. Flop K♥ J♥ 9♠ (two broadway cards, drawy). You have Q♣ 8♦ (nothing but a gutshot to the nut straight).
question: This player is 'tight' by preflop stats, but their actual postflop tendency is to never fold once in a hand. Which read should drive your c-bet decision?
explanation: Fold-to-cbet is a postflop stat, and it doesn't automatically follow from a player being tight preflop — those measure different decisions entirely. A player can easily be selective about which hands they play and still refuse to fold any of them once they've committed to seeing a flop. Check or bet small purely for the backup equity, not for fold equity — don't borrow a 'tight players fold' assumption from the wrong stat; use what you've actually observed them do postflop.

scenario: You raise BTN, BB calls — you are in position. Flop 8♣ 5♠ 2♥ (dry, low, disconnected). You have K♥ 6♥ (king-high, backdoor flush draw only, no pair).
question: In position, marginal backdoor-only hand, dry low board. Is betting or checking back the better default?
options: Always bet — never check in position
Bet big to end it now
Check back — free card, no risk
explanation: Being in position doesn't mean betting more of your weakest hands — it means you have the option to check back cheaply and still see the next card for free, without the risk a check carries out of position (facing a bet you can't profitably continue against). With a hand this marginal (king-high, no pair, just a backdoor draw), that free look is often worth more than the thin fold equity a bet would generate. Check back — position is most valuable as the ability to control the pot for free, not as a green light to bet everything.
